content: Cetirizine hydrochloride is an antihistamine and a major metabolite of hydroxyzine. It is a racemic selective H1 receptor antagonist that is commonly used to treat allergies, hay fever, angioedema, and urticaria. Its structural similarity to hydroxyzine and its derivation from piperazine contribute to its similar adverse effects and properties as other piperazine derivatives. Cetirizine is available in chewable tablets, non-chewable tablets, and syrup formulations. These forms are rapidly and effectively absorbed, with food having only a minimal effect on the absorption rate. Peak serum levels are typically achieved approximately one hour after administration. In a study involving healthy volunteers who were given 10 mg of cetirizine daily for 10 days, the mean peak serum concentration was found to be 311 ng/mL. Cetirizine has a long duration of action, remaining in the body for up to 21 hours before being excreted. Its average elimination half-life is approximately 8 hours. Around 70% of the drug is excreted via the kidneys within 72 hours, with 10% being eliminated through urine or feces, half of which is in the form of unchanged cetirizine. Cetirizine is often combined with pseudoephedrine hydrochloride, a decongestant, in medications marketed under the same brand name with a -D suffix (e.g., Zyrtec-D, Virlix-D). This combination is commonly used to address both allergic symptoms and nasal congestion. In some cases, cetirizine may be prescribed to individuals in institutional settings who suffer from depression, as it can temporarily enhance emotions such as alertness, speediness, and even anger. However, repeated use may increase the likelihood of these emotional effects. The active enantiomer of cetirizine, known as levocetirizine, is marketed under the brand names Xyzal and Xusal. Levocetirizine is reported to have a slightly reduced side effect profile compared to cetirizine. Cetirizine has demonstrated efficacy in the treatment of Kimura's disease, a rare condition that primarily affects young Asian men. This disease involves tumor-like lesions in the lymph nodes and soft tissues of the head and neck. Cetirizine's dual properties as an anti-inflammatory agent and an effective treatment for pruritus make it particularly suitable for managing the pruritus associated with these lesions. In a 2005 study conducted by the American College of Rheumatology, a patient with Kimura's disease was initially treated with prednisone, followed by a regimen of steroids, azathioprine, omeprazole, and calcium and vitamin D supplements over a two-year period. While the patient's skin condition improved and the lesions diminished, side effects such as cushingoid features and hirsutism were observed. The patient was subsequently transitioned to a 10 mg/day dose of cetirizine to prevent further skin lesions. Following this change, the patient's skin lesions resolved asymptomatically, blood eosinophil counts normalized, corticosteroid-related side effects subsided, and remission was achieved within two months. It is hypothesized that the inhibition of eosinophils plays a critical role in the treatment of Kimura's disease, as eosinophils are believed to be more directly involved in the development of the skin lesions than other cell types.
